title: Non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome (NSTEMI and unstable angina)
subject: cardiology
summary: Confirm with serial high-sensitivity troponin, stratify risk, give aspirin and a parenteral anticoagulant, time angiography to risk (within 2 hours if very high risk, within 24 hours if high risk, otherwise selective), and use DAPT for 12 months by default.

sections.title: Recognise and diagnose
items: Ischaemic chest discomfort at rest, new-onset or crescendo angina, or equivalents (breathlessness, epigastric pain, sweating), without persistent ST elevation.

ECG within 10 minutes and repeat with recurrent symptoms. It may show ST depression, transient ST elevation or T-wave inversion, or be normal. Record V7 to V9 and V3R to V4R if non-diagnostic: circumflex occlusion can be ECG-silent.

NSTEMI: rise and/or fall of cardiac troponin with at least one value above the 99th percentile, plus clinical evidence of ischaemia. Unstable angina: ischaemic symptoms at rest or minimal effort without troponin elevation.
Use high-sensitivity troponin with the assay-specific ESC 0 h/1 h (or 0 h/2 h) algorithm. If the first two values are inconclusive and suspicion persists, repeat at 3 hours and consider echo.
Consider alternatives and type 2 MI: aortic dissection, pulmonary embolism, myopericarditis, Takotsubo, and supply-demand mismatch (anaemia, tachyarrhythmia, sepsis, hypertensive emergency).

sections.title: Initial management
items: Continuous ECG monitoring. Oxygen only if SpO2 is below 90%. Sublingual or IV nitrate for ongoing angina (avoid with hypotension, RV infarction or recent PDE5 inhibitor).
Aspirin 150 to 300 mg orally (non-enteric-coated) loading, then 75 to 100 mg daily, for all without contraindication.

Parenteral anticoagulant at diagnosis: UFH or enoxaparin if angiography is planned within 24 hours. Fondaparinux 2.5 mg SC daily is preferred if angiography is not expected within 24 hours (a full UFH bolus is given at PCI).
Do not routinely pretreat with a P2Y12 inhibitor when angiography is planned within 24 hours and anatomy is unknown. If angiography will be delayed, pretreatment may be considered.
Start a high-intensity statin early. Oral beta-blocker for ongoing ischaemia if there is no heart failure, hypotension, bradycardia or AV block.

sections.title: Risk stratification and invasive timing
items: Very high risk: immediate angiography (within 2 hours): haemodynamic instability or cardiogenic shock, recurrent or refractory chest pain despite medical treatment, life-threatening arrhythmias, mechanical complications, acute heart failure due to ischaemia, recurrent dynamic ST or T changes (especially intermittent ST elevation).
High risk: early angiography (within 24 hours): NSTEMI confirmed by troponin, dynamic ST or T changes, transient ST elevation, or GRACE risk score above 140.
Other patients (for example suspected unstable angina with normal troponin and ECG): selective invasive strategy guided by non-invasive testing (stress imaging or CT coronary angiography).

Bloods: serial hs-troponin, CBC, creatinine and eGFR (for contrast and drug dosing), electrolytes, glucose and HbA1c, lipids. Echocardiography for LV function, regional wall motion and mechanical complications.
Assess bleeding risk (ARC-HBR criteria: age 75 or older, anaemia, CKD, prior bleeding, oral anticoagulation, thrombocytopenia) to guide drug choice and DAPT duration.

sections.title: Antithrombotic therapy
items: DAPT: aspirin plus prasugrel or ticagrelor. Prasugrel should be considered in preference to ticagrelor in patients proceeding to PCI; ticagrelor if managed without PCI. Clopidogrel if both are contraindicated or unavailable, or if oral anticoagulation is needed.
Stop parenteral anticoagulation after PCI unless there is another indication (AF, LV thrombus, VTE). Do not switch between UFH and enoxaparin.

Default DAPT 12 months. High bleeding risk: consider single antiplatelet therapy after 1 month. Event-free patients without high ischaemic risk may step down to a single antiplatelet (preferably a P2Y12 inhibitor) after 3 to 6 months.

Patients on oral anticoagulation (for example AF): aspirin plus OAC plus clopidogrel for up to 1 week, then OAC plus clopidogrel up to 12 months, then OAC alone. Prefer a DOAC over a VKA and add a PPI.
GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors only as bailout during PCI (no-reflow or thrombotic complication).

sections.title: Revascularisation and discharge
items: PCI or CABG by coronary anatomy; Heart Team discussion for left main or multivessel disease, particularly with diabetes or reduced LVEF.
High-intensity statin with LDL-C goal below 55 mg/dL (1.4 mmol/L) and at least 50% reduction; add ezetimibe, then a PCSK9 inhibitor, if not at goal.
LVEF 40% or less: beta-blocker, ACE inhibitor (ARB if intolerant) and MRA, plus an SGLT2 inhibitor if heart failure. Smoking cessation, BP and diabetes control, cardiac rehabilitation.
Low-risk patients with negative serial hs-troponin, a normal ECG and no ongoing pain can be discharged with early outpatient functional or anatomical testing.

sections.title: Special situations
items: CKD: enoxaparin 1 mg/kg once daily if eGFR 15 to 29 and avoid below 15 (use UFH); fondaparinux is contraindicated if eGFR is below 20. Minimise contrast volume.
Elderly: offer the same invasive strategy if fit; dose by weight and renal function; clopidogrel is reasonable in high bleeding risk.
Non-obstructive coronaries (MINOCA): look for myocarditis, Takotsubo, spontaneous coronary dissection, coronary spasm or embolism, usually with cardiac MRI.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Ruling out on a single troponin taken early after symptom onset when the validated hs-troponin algorithm does not allow it.
Routine prasugrel or ticagrelor pretreatment before early angiography: more bleeding, no benefit.
Treating type 2 MI (anaemia, sepsis, tachyarrhythmia) as type 1 with aggressive antithrombotics instead of correcting the cause.
Full-dose enoxaparin in severe renal impairment or the very elderly without dose adjustment.

drugs.name: Aspirin
drugs.dose: 150 to 300 mg orally loading, then 75 to 100 mg once daily

drugs.name: Prasugrel
drugs.dose: 60 mg orally loading at PCI, then 10 mg once daily; 5 mg daily if 75 years or older or weight under 60 kg
drugs.notes: Contraindicated after previous stroke or TIA.

drugs.name: Ticagrelor
drugs.dose: 180 mg orally loading, then 90 mg twice daily
drugs.notes: Dyspnoea is common and usually benign. Avoid after intracranial haemorrhage.

drugs.name: Clopidogrel
drugs.dose: 300 to 600 mg orally loading, then 75 mg once daily
drugs.notes: For patients on oral anticoagulation or when potent agents are contraindicated.

drugs.name: Fondaparinux
drugs.notes: Preferred when angiography is not expected within 24 hours. Give a full UFH bolus at PCI. Contraindicated if eGFR below 20.

drugs.name: Enoxaparin
drugs.notes: eGFR 15 to 29: 1 mg/kg once daily; avoid below 15.

drugs.name: Unfractionated heparin (UFH)
drugs.dose: 60 to 70 IU/kg IV bolus (max 5000 IU), then 12 to 15 IU/kg/h (max 1000 IU/h), aPTT 1.5 to 2.5 times control; at PCI 70 to 100 IU/kg IV, ACT-guided

drugs.name: Atorvastatin (or rosuvastatin)
drugs.dose: Atorvastatin 40 to 80 mg orally once daily (or rosuvastatin 20 to 40 mg once daily)

drugs.name: Isosorbide dinitrate or glyceryl trinitrate
drugs.dose: Isosorbide dinitrate 5 mg sublingual, or glyceryl trinitrate 0.4 to 0.5 mg sublingual, repeated every 5 minutes up to 3 doses
drugs.notes: IV glyceryl trinitrate for persistent pain or hypertension. Avoid if SBP below 90 mmHg or PDE5 inhibitor in the last 24 to 48 hours.
